candidate.summary: Pulse Local, a Mac budgeting app whose AI models run on your machine. Hi HN, I'm Niz. Pulse Local is a budgeting app for Mac (Apple Silicon, beta) that answers questions about your spending with models that run on your machine. Local mode needs no account. The ledger and your questions stay on the machine, and the app sends no analytics or crash logs. I felt there are not enough consumer apps that run locally with no calls to the outside world that help us manage sensitive corners of our lives. This app in its local variant only downloads a couple of models and occasional updates, it does not send any analytics nor data. Features-wise, Pulse local is a complete budgeting app that offers an assistant built on top of a fine-tuned model and thousands of rules embedded in the code itself. I'm sharing it for free with options to help me continue experimenting with fine-tuning and expanding along this direction. How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. When you ask a question, a tuned Qwen3 0.6B model reads it into a structured query, and code, not the model, does the money math against the ledger. evidence.excerpt:
Very nice project. I think this is is in the step of the right direction for agent-driven assistance. > How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. I think this is where you're going to lose people. If you're having to pull in data from multiple different sources, each with their own flow for exporting, I think this might be a non-starter for creating good financial habbit. I recnetly had success integrating my local AI agent with Monarch money via an open source monarch MCP project. It took a bit of (AI) hacking the login stuff, but now I'm able to pull transactions, query patterns, have a daily report generated from hermes, etc. Much more technical that your target audience but possibly offers some inspiration.
Your domain name is younger than 30 days old so my firewall blocks it. :/
Very cool. What does it use the model for? Could you replace it with something lighter, like some classifiers[0]? Or do you need the chat? Besides the chat, what other tasks is the model used for? Thank you! https://jeffyclassify.com/blog/when-llms-fail-at-classificat...
I use budgeting apps on a daily basis, and I'll just share my personal feedback: I'm absolutely not downloading ~3 gigs for a budget app. Everything I need to "ask" the app is already available to me in the form of reports, charts, and tables. I don't really have many open-ended questions about my budget because anything important to track is already handled deterministically. Also yes, it's local but the data you're importing is already with a private organization on the cloud. In that sense, having a local copy of it does not really do anything for me in terms of privacy etc. As I said, I use budgeting apps daily (one for personal use (self-made), another for business (very old freenium era software that has not failed me in the last 5+ years of self-hosting it)) and I do not see any need for generative AI in that workflow from my pov. YMMV
I love the idea of local only apps woth no network comms. I do wish macOS had some way you could enforce that out of the box though. Rather than trust the claims of the developer. Another app I love that does the same. Queryable which lets you natural language search your photos on device on iOS and predates most of the current AI craze (2022) and also apple adding this themselves to photos: https://queryable.app/

evidence.title: How Pulse Local works
evidence.excerpt:
How Pulse Local works
Pulse Local is a budgeting app for your desktop. It needs no account, and your questions never go to an online AI service.
Here is what it does with your transactions, and how it answers you.
For Pulse Local 0.4.21 · Updated 25 October 2026 · Mac with Apple Silicon today, Windows next
Start with your transactions.
Import the file your bank gives you: CSV, Excel, OFX, QIF, MT940 and other bank formats, or a PDF statement in beta. Monarch Money, YNAB and Copilot exports import too. Pulse reads the file on your machine. When it is not sure of a sign, a date or the currency, it tells you before it saves anything. Each account keeps its own currency, and no total adds two currencies.
Check the categories and set a monthly target for anything you want to watch. Spending shows what you have used and what is left.
Split a shared purchase across categories. Set a rule once for a shop you use often. The rule remembers the shop, not the whole bank line, so next month's charge gets the same category. Before you save a rule, Pulse shows the past transactions it matches. Carry unused budget into next month. Analysis compares months and shows where the money went.
Set up your first budget
Ask a question. Check what was counted.
Ask “How much did I spend on groceries in August?” For spending questions it supports, Pulse finds the transactions and adds them up itself, so the AI does not guess the total. A second small model also reads your question, and you see a figure only when both agree. The app calls this Better understanding. It is on by default on every machine.
Labels above the answer show the month and category Pulse used. Change one to adjust the question, ask “by merchant” for a breakdown, or open Transactions to see the purchases.
Pulse can still misread you. A glance at the labels catches an answer about the wrong month or the wrong kind of spending. Chat works best in English; screens are in English or Japanese.
Help with everyday terms
Ask “What is a sinking fund?” and Pulse gives a ready-written explanation. It explains the idea and leaves the decision to you.
Other questions may go to a small AI model on your machine. Its answers are labelled. Check any figure in them.
More ways to ask Pulse
Your conversations stay with you.
Your transactions, your chats and the AI all stay on your machine. The first start downloads the AI models once: about
MB in all, the money check included. You can switch the check off in Settings. After that, Local mode works offline. Update checks are optional.
Connected mode is optional. It brings in transactions from US banks on its own, through Plaid, a bank-connection service, and needs the Sync Pass: $29 a year for three banks, $8 a year for each extra, up to 25. Transactions and balances pass through our server to your machine. They are processed, not stored. We keep only what the connection and your pass need.
See what is shared and what stays private
Where Pulse can go wrong.
Pulse knows only what you give it. It cannot see a transaction you never imported, look up a live price, or know what never reaches your bank. A forecast is an estimate, and any answer can be wrong.
When Pulse cannot back an answer with your records, or its two readings of your question disagree, it holds the answer back and tells you. We test it on made-up households and questions it has never seen.
Before you rely on an answer
The few things worth checking, and what to do when an answer looks wrong.
How we test the chat
What failed in testing, the check we built, and what a later sealed test showed.
The AI on your machine
Two small open models, free for anyone to download. Pulse’s own code answers the questions it supports. A model tuned for budgeting answers the rest, with a label. The second model checks money answers; it is on by default on every machine.
Model files on Hugging Face
Ready to try your first budget?

Nothing here is financial advice.

Download a file of your transactions from your bank.
In Pulse Local, choose

Read the notes above the preview. They tell you how Pulse read the file and what it is not sure of.

Pulse reads the file on your machine. The file is not uploaded.
CSV, Excel, OFX, QFX, QIF, MT940, CAMT.053, Norma 43 from Spanish banks, CODA from Belgian banks, OFC from Microsoft Money and statement files from FNB in South Africa. PDF statements are in beta: check every row before you import.
Pulse looks at what is in the file, not at its name. A CSV that your bank saves with an .xls or .dat name imports as a CSV. A web page table that your bank saves with an .xls name imports too.
Bank files from any country.
Columns in any order, column names in many languages, commas or semicolons, decimal commas, day-first dates, accents and long account numbers. Pulse also reads files saved in Japanese Shift_JIS, in Chinese GBK or in older Windows formats. Short bank names such as WHOLEFDS still find the shop.
Pulse knows more column names in Norwegian, Polish, Czech, Finnish, Estonian, Latvian, Hungarian, Korean, Chinese and Japanese, and columns named DR and CR. It also knows more names for money in and money out, such as Дебет and Кредит, DARE and AVERE, Saída and Entrada, and ghi nợ and ghi có. It reads dates with the name of the month, such as 3 févr. 2025 or 24 lug 2024, and dates such as 2026年3月12日.
A currency mark beside the amount.
Pulse reads amounts such as 10,000원, 45,10 zł, 500 Kč and R$ 45,10. A mark that only one currency uses names the file’s currency.
Column names Pulse does not know.
If a file has no column names, or if Pulse does not know the name of the date or amount column, Pulse reads those columns from their values and tells you. Check the preview.
A short file under a long heading.
Some banks put many lines of account details above a few transactions. Pulse finds the transactions below them. If a line above the column names looks like a transaction, Pulse leaves it out and tells you.
Money in and money out in two columns.
Pulse also reads the two columns when their names give the side in brackets, such as Amount (in) and Amount (out). If one row has an amount in both columns, such as a time deposit renewed with its interest, Pulse counts the difference.
American Express, Chase and Capital One files are read the right way round. Other card files are too, when their own payment or refund rows show which way round they are. In a card file, a currency that shows only on purchases abroad does not change the account’s currency.
Other budgeting apps.
Monarch Money, YNAB and Copilot exports import with their categories. Each one lands in the matching Pulse category, in any of 31 languages, or stays as your own. A category that only holds money coming in is kept as income.
What the import tells you
Pulse does not guess in silence. When it is not sure about a file, it tells you on the import sheet before it saves anything.
Pulse looks for the currency in the columns, the column names, the account or card name, the heading, the lines below the rows, the account number and the file name. If the amounts show only $ and a country column names a country with another dollar, such as Canada, Pulse tells you that the file is likely in that dollar. If the file is in another currency, Pulse asks before it imports. If the file names no currency, Pulse tells you that the amounts land in your ledger’s currency as written.
Several currencies use $, and two use ¥. So when a file shows only $ or ¥ and your ledger uses the same mark, the file does not name its currency. Pulse tells you so in one short line. Marks such as R$, A$, CA$, zł and 원 name one currency.
If each date in the file can be read two ways, Pulse tells you the order

verified_facts: Pulse Local 是一款面向 Mac（Apple Silicon，beta）的预算应用，其 AI 模型在本地机器上运行。
本地模式不需要账户，账本和用户提问都留在本机，应用不发送分析数据或崩溃日志。
首次启动会一次性下载约 830 MB 的 AI 模型，其中包括一个用于复核金额答案的小模型，可在设置中关闭。
应用会检查是否有新版本并下载更新，该功能也可关闭；除此之外不发送其他数据。
用户可从任意银行导入 CSV 等文件，支持多种格式（CSV、Excel、OFX、QFX、QIF、MT940、CAMT.053、Norma 43、CODA，PDF 对账单为 beta）。
每个账户保留自己的货币，不会把两种货币相加或换算。
提问时，一个经过微调的 Qwen3 0.6B 模型把问题解析为结构化查询，由代码（而非模型）对账本做金额计算。
第二个 4B 复核模型会复核每个金额答案；只有两个模型结果一致时才显示数字，该功能默认开启。
官方称在 387 段未见过的对话上测试，开启复核时错误数字答案的比例低于关闭时（具体数值在摘录中被截断）。
可选的 Connected 模式通过 Plaid 同步美国银行交易，需要 Sync Pass：每年 29 美元含三家银行，每增加一家每年 8 美元，最多 25 家。
同步时交易和余额经服务器传递到本机，服务器只保留连接令牌及银行、状态、最后同步时间等记录，不存储交易数据。
应用界面支持英语和日语，聊天以英语效果最佳；本地模式全球可用，同步目前仅限美国。
